Course: Information Security (week 2, topic: password storage, status: KNOWN).

Question: My tutor says my answer on password storage is not complete. Describe password storage and justify the choice you would make. Which points am I losing and why?

Student answer: MD5 and SHA-256 are built to be fast, so a cracker can test billions of candidate passwords per second. each account gets its own random salt, so one precomputed table cannot cover every account at once. store the value with bcrypt or Argon2 rather than a plain hash. the cost parameter has to be raised as hardware gets faster.

Official rubric points:
1. Says a general-purpose hash is unsuitable because it is fast
2. Names a per-user salt and says what it defeats
3. Names a deliberately slow password hash
4. Says the work factor is tuned and raised over time

Verdict: correct (4/4) - nothing to repair, so I will push you further instead.

Earned, with the words that earned them:
- Point 1 (Says a general-purpose hash is unsuitable because it is fast): "MD5 and SHA-256 are built to be fast, so a cracker can test billions of candidate passwords per second"
- Point 2 (Names a per-user salt and says what it defeats): "each account gets its own random salt, so one precomputed table cannot cover every account at once"
- Point 3 (Names a deliberately slow password hash): "store the value with bcrypt or Argon2 rather than a plain hash"
- Point 4 (Says the work factor is tuned and raised over time): "the cost parameter has to be raised as hardware gets faster"

The next level of this: you have the rule; the place people lose it later is under pressure, when that a password hash is judged by how unbreakable the algorithm sounds, when the property that matters is how slow it is per guess creeps back in. Your answer already rules that out, so keep the sentence that does it.

My 1.5 gb monthly bundle costs more than i want to spend and video lectures finish it in three days, so I want to get this right in one pass.

Student answer: MD5 and SHA-256 are built to be fast, so a cracker can test billions of candidate passwords per second. store the value with bcrypt or Argon2 rather than a plain hash. the cost parameter has to be raised as hardware gets faster.

Official rubric points:
1. Says a general-purpose hash is unsuitable because it is fast
2. Names a per-user salt and says what it defeats
3. Names a deliberately slow password hash
4. Says the work factor is tuned and raised over time

Verdict: partially_correct. You earn 3 of 4; here is exactly where the other 1 went.

Earned, quoted from your answer:
- Point 1 (Says a general-purpose hash is unsuitable because it is fast): "MD5 and SHA-256 are built to be fast, so a cracker can test billions of candidate passwords per second"

- Point 4 (Says the work factor is tuned and raised over time): "the cost parameter has to be raised as hardware gets faster"

Not earned, because nothing in your answer covers them:
- Point 2: Names a per-user salt and says what it defeats

Named plainly, the wrong idea is this: that a password hash is judged by how unbreakable the algorithm sounds, when the property that matters is how slow it is per guess.
The correct statement: Replace the fast hash with bcrypt or Argon2 at a tuned cost factor, and give every account its own random salt.
The reason underneath: An attacker who steals the table guesses offline, so your only lever is the time each guess costs: a fast hash gives them billions per second, a tuned bcrypt gives them a few thousand.

To prove the fix stuck: Take your current code, swap the hash for bcrypt with a cost factor you time on your own machine, and write down how many guesses per second that cost buys the attacker. Password hashing is a cost problem, not a secrecy problem. The attacker who dumps your table runs guesses offline, so the defence is to make each guess expensive: a slow KDF (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2) with a tuned work factor, plus a per-user random salt so one table of precomputed hashes cannot be reused across accounts. Hashing twice with MD5 doubles a cost that was near zero.

Before I go further - You called it one-way, and it is. So where exactly does an attacker who already has the whole table spend their time?
I think the answer is that MD5 and SHA-256 are built to be fast, so a cracker can test billions of candidate passwords per second.

Yes - that is the load-bearing half, and you got to it from the record rather than from memory, which is the habit that scores.

What your sentence leaves implicit: Replace the fast hash with bcrypt or Argon2 at a tuned cost factor, and give every account its own random salt. An attacker who steals the table guesses offline, so your only lever is the time each guess costs: a fast hash gives them billions per second, a tuned bcrypt gives them a few thousand.

Now apply it where it is less obvious: A colleague suggests storing SHA-256(password + a single site-wide secret pepper). Say which of the two problems that fixes, which it does not, and why.

Symmetric ciphers are fast but need a key both sides already hold - that is the distribution problem. Asymmetric crypto solves distribution, because a public key can be published, but it is slow and size-limited. So real systems are hybrid: public-key crypto agrees a fresh symmetric session key, and everything after that is symmetric. Strength is not what selects between them; who-knows-what-when is.

Something like: the handshake exchanges a symmetric key with public-key crypto, then the traffic is AES?

Close, and it is the right end of the problem. Said precisely: Use public-key crypto only to agree on a key, then encrypt the actual data with a symmetric cipher.

The reason that phrasing matters: Public-key operations cost orders of magnitude more per byte than a block cipher, so the pair is used for the one small secret that cannot be shared in advance and the cheap cipher does the bulk work.

3. Says stored data is a separate problem
4. Mentions certificate identity binding

The splice itself is O(1) in a list and O(n) in an array, but the locate step reverses that: O(n) for the list, O(1) for the array. Lists pay off when you already hold the position (an iterator, a node you kept, a head or tail push) or when the elements are large and copying dominates. binary search tree balance in Data Structures - try 12. I have been at this for a while. What I have so far: A BST stores values in sorted order. Just tell me the answer?

Right: no more questions, here is the answer with the reasoning attached.

Search in a BST costs one comparison per level, so the real quantity is height. Height depends on insertion order: random or balanced input gives about log n, ascending input gives a chain of n. That is why self-balancing variants exist - AVL and red-black trees perform rotations on insert to bound the height, paying a small constant to keep the logarithm true in the worst case.
Okay. So was binary search trees are o(log n) for search because they halve the data at every step, so the order you insert in does not matter completely wrong, or just incomplete?

Incomplete rather than random - it is a reasonable reading of the evidence you had. The specific thing that makes it fail: Each comparison eliminates one subtree, so you pay one step per level; only a balanced shape keeps the number of levels near log n.

Try this: Given a BST that has degenerated into a chain, describe what an AVL rotation would do at the first violating node and which property it restores.
Would a self-balancing tree such as an AVL or red-black tree rotates to keep the height logarithmic count as an answer?

That counts, and it is the right shape. The one thing I would add for full marks: Tie the cost to height and the height to insertion order: insert sorted keys into a plain BST and you have built a linked list with extra pointers.

Keep that sentence - it is the difference between recognising this and being able to use it.

Search in a BST costs one comparison per level, so the real quantity is height. Height depends on insertion order: random or balanced input gives about log n, ascending input gives a chain of n. That is why self-balancing variants exist - AVL and red-black trees perform rotations on insert to bound the height, paying a small constant to keep the logarithm true in the worst case.

Before I go further - Draw the tree you get by inserting 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in that order. How many comparisons does it take to find 5?

Each comparison eliminates one subtree, so you pay one step per level; only a balanced shape keeps the number of levels near log n.

Question: We were asked about recursion, base cases and stack depth in Algorithms. Set out recursion, base cases and stack depth and the condition where it breaks. Mark my answer against the official points, please.

Student answer: There has to be a case that returns without recursing, and every path must reach it. each call has to move the argument towards the base case. every pending call keeps a frame, so deep recursion exhausts the stack even when it is finite. convert to iteration with an explicit stack, or use tail recursion where the language supports it.

Official rubric points:
1. Says a base case must be reachable for every input
2. Says the recursive call must shrink the problem
3. Explains stack overflow as depth, not as an infinite loop
4. Mentions an alternative for deep cases

Verdict: correct (4/4) - nothing to repair, so I will push you further instead.

Earned, with the words that earned them:
- Point 1 (Says a base case must be reachable for every input): "there has to be a case that returns without recursing, and every path must reach it"
- Point 2 (Says the recursive call must shrink the problem): "each call has to move the argument towards the base case"
- Point 3 (Explains stack overflow as depth, not as an infinite loop): "every pending call keeps a frame, so deep recursion exhausts the stack even when it is finite"
- Point 4 (Mentions an alternative for deep cases): "convert to iteration with an explicit stack, or use tail recursion where the language supports it"

The next level of this: you have the rule; the place people lose it later is under pressure, when that a stack overflow means the recursion never ends, when a perfectly terminating recursion can still be too deep creeps back in. Course: Algorithms (week 8, topic: recursion, base cases and stack depth, status: KNOWN).

Question: I answered this in the Algorithms quiz and got it back with no comments. Describe recursion, base cases and stack depth and justify the choice you would make. What would a marker say?

Student answer: There has to be a case that returns without recursing, and every path must reach it. each call has to move the argument towards the base case. every pending call keeps a frame, so deep recursion exhausts the stack even when it is finite. convert to iteration with an explicit stack, or use tail recursion where the language supports it.

Greedy makes an irrevocable local choice; DP keeps every subproblem answer so no branch is lost. Greedy is not a faster DP - it is a bet that the greedy-choice property holds, and it must be proved (exchange argument) or checked against counterexamples. Coin change with 1, 3, 4 breaks it: greedy makes 6 as 4+1+1, the optimum is 3+3. When subproblems overlap and no exchange argument exists, DP with memoisation is the safe structure.

Normal forms are defined by functional dependencies, not by table count. 1NF: atomic values. 2NF: no non-key attribute depends on part of a composite key. 3NF: no non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute. An index is a separate sorted structure, usually a B-tree, kept in sync with the table. Reads on a selective predicate get to jump straight to the rows; every write pays to maintain each index. The planner will skip an index when the predicate hides the column inside a function, when a leading wildcard defeats the ordering, or when selectivity is so low that a scan is cheaper. So the design question is which predicates are hot and selective, not which columns exist.

Before I go further - You added an index to every column. What happens now on each INSERT, and how many structures must be updated?
I think the answer is that an index lets the engine find matching rows without scanning the table.

Yes - that is the load-bearing half, and you got to it from the record rather than from memory, which is the habit that scores.

What your sentence leaves implicit: Index the columns your predicates actually filter on, and account for the write cost you are adding to every insert and update. An index is a sorted structure maintained alongside the table, so each write touches both, and the planner only uses it when the predicate can be expressed as a range over that structure.

An index is a separate sorted structure, usually a B-tree, kept in sync with the table. Reads on a selective predicate get to jump straight to the rows; every write pays to maintain each index. A transaction gives atomicity and durability for your group of writes, but concurrent correctness comes from isolation. At read-committed, two sessions that read the same row, compute, and write back will silently lose one update - the transaction boundary does not stop it. Fixes, cheapest first: a single atomic statement (UPDATE balance = balance + 100), an explicit SELECT FOR UPDATE, an optimistic version column, or raising the isolation level and handling the aborts.

Before I go further - Both sessions read the balance as 500, add 100 and write 600. Which part of ACID was supposed to stop that, and did it?

What your sentence leaves implicit: Name the anomaly you are preventing and choose the mechanism for it: atomicity groups the writes, but concurrent correctness needs the right isolation level or an explicit lock. Atomicity is about what survives a failure; isolation is about what a concurrent transaction is allowed to see, and at read-committed two sessions can each read, compute and write, losing one result.

Question: What is the one thing I have to understand about join types?

Start from what the record commits you to. [lecture#db-w6-joins] says: Week 6: every join in the assignment must be justified by which rows it must preserve. That sentence is the standard your answer will be marked against, so everything below serves it.

Joins differ in which unmatched rows survive. Inner keeps only pairs; left keeps every left row and pads the right with nulls. The classic trap is a left join followed by WHERE right.status = 'paid': null rows fail that predicate, so the outer join silently collapses to an inner one. Move the condition into the ON clause when you want it to filter the match rather than the result, and index the join key so the engine is not hashing the whole table.

Before I go further - Your report should list every customer, including those who ordered nothing. Which of those customers can an inner join return?
I think the answer is that rows without a partner on the other side disappear.

Yes - that is the load-bearing half, and you got to it from the record rather than from memory, which is the habit that scores.

What your sentence leaves implicit: Pick the join by the rows you must keep, then keep right-side conditions in the ON clause so the outer join survives. An inner join is a filter as well as a combination: any left row with no matching key is dropped, which is exactly the count difference you are seeing.

Now apply it where it is less obvious: Write the query that lists customers with no orders at all, and say which join and which predicate does that work.

TCP buys reliability and ordering with acknowledgements, retransmission and congestion control - and pays in latency and head-of-line blocking: everything behind a lost segment waits. For a file that is correct; for a live call it is a stall you can hear, and the retransmitted audio is useless by arrival. UDP hands the application the raw datagram service so it can conceal loss instead (jitter buffers, forward error correction, concealment). It is a trade, not a ranking.

DNS is a distributed lookup: resolver to root, to the TLD servers, to the domain's authoritative server, with caching at every hop governed by each record's TTL. It is usually milliseconds and it happens once per name per TTL - the page content never passes through it. Two consequences worth remembering: slow pages are almost never DNS after the first request, and record changes propagate only as fast as cached copies expire, so you lower the TTL before a migration, not during it.

What your sentence leaves implicit: Separate the lookup from the transfer: DNS answers once, usually in milliseconds, and the page bytes then travel over a connection DNS never touches. Because answers are cached for the record's TTL, a change propagates only as fast as the old copies expire, which is why a cutover is planned by lowering the TTL in advance.

Question: For the Computer Networks revision sheet on bandwidth versus latency: explain bandwidth versus latency well enough that someone could act on it. Where does this answer stop being right?

Student answer: Bandwidth is how many bits per second the link can carry. latency is how long a single packet takes to get there and back. a wider link does not shorten the distance, so the round trip stays the same. a page with many small round trips feels slow even on a fast link.

Official rubric points:
1. Defines bandwidth as throughput per unit time
2. Defines latency as one-way or round-trip delay
3. Says more bandwidth does not reduce round-trip time
4. Identifies a latency-bound workload

Bandwidth and latency are independent. Bandwidth is bits per second - it decides how long a large transfer takes. Latency is the delay of a single trip, set mostly by distance, queueing and processing, and it does not improve when the pipe widens. A page with many dependent small requests is latency-bound: its floor is the number of sequential round trips times the round-trip time. That is why bundling, caching, connection reuse and moving content closer help where extra megabits do not.

Before I go further - Your link goes from 10 to 100 megabits. What happens to the time for one 200-byte request and its reply?

What your sentence leaves implicit: Measure which one binds first: count the round trips your page needs and multiply by the round-trip time before buying capacity. Bandwidth widens the pipe but the propagation and queueing delay of each round trip is unchanged, so a page made of 60 dependent small requests is limited by 60 times the round-trip time.

The defining difference is the address space. Threads share one, so communication is a variable assignment - fast, and unsafe without synchronisation, because a read-modify-write can interleave. Processes have separate spaces, so a fault or a memory corruption is contained and communication must be explicit (pipes, sockets, shared memory you opt into). 'Lightweight' describes the creation cost; the semantics are what should drive the choice.

Before I go further - Your two workers update the same total and the total is wrong. What can a thread reach that a separate process could not?

What your sentence leaves implicit: Lead with the shared address space: threads share memory, which is both the speed advantage and the reason your counter is corrupted. Two threads incrementing the same variable interleave a read-modify-write, so an update can be lost; two processes cannot do this because neither can see the other's memory.

Alternatives are all-or-nothing acquisition, or timeouts with rollback, which trade certainty for simplicity. Detect-and-restart leaves the structure intact and the bug returns under load.

Course: Operating Systems (week 2, topic: virtual memory and paging, status: KNOWN).

Question: Before the Operating Systems test, grade this for me. Describe virtual memory and paging and justify the choice you would make. Be strict.

Student answer: Addresses in a program are virtual and translated to physical frames. the hardware translates page numbers to frames using the page table. a page not in memory triggers a fault and is fetched from disk. if the working set does not fit, the system spends its time paging instead of running.

Official rubric points:
1. Says each process sees its own virtual address space
2. Says the MMU and page table perform translation
3. Says pages can be backed by disk, causing page faults
4. Says thrashing is excessive paging, not slow disk alone

Verdict: correct - 4 of 4 points, and the reasoning is yours.

Earned, with the words that earned them:
- Point 1 (Says each process sees its own virtual address space): "addresses in a program are virtual and translated to physical frames"
- Point 2 (Says the MMU and page table perform translation): "the hardware translates page numbers to frames using the page table"
- Point 3 (Says pages can be backed by disk, causing page faults): "a page not in memory triggers a fault and is fetched from disk"
- Point 4 (Says thrashing is excessive paging, not slow disk alone): "if the working set does not fit, the system spends its time paging instead of running"

The next level of this: you have the rule; the place people lose it later is under pressure, when that virtual memory is simply extra RAM provided by the disk, so adding swap is equivalent to adding memory creeps back in. Your answer already rules that out, so keep the sentence that does it.

Start from what the record commits you to. [lecture#os-w6-memory] says: Week 6: answers must separate the address-space abstraction from the swapping mechanism. That sentence is the standard your answer will be marked against, so everything below serves it.

Virtual memory is an address-translation and isolation mechanism: every process sees a private space, the MMU translates pages to frames, and pages that do not fit can be backed by disk. Swap is an overflow valve, not capacity - a fault costs on the order of milliseconds against nanoseconds for RAM. When the working set exceeds physical memory the system thrashes: nearly all time goes into paging. So the design question is the size of the active working set, not the sum of RAM and swap.

Before I go further - Your program's hot data is 3 GB and RAM is 2 GB. What does the machine do on each access to the missing part?
I think the answer is that addresses in a program are virtual and translated to physical frames.

What your sentence leaves implicit: Say what virtual memory actually provides - address translation and isolation - and treat swap as a slow overflow whose cost is page faults, not as capacity. A page fault costs something like a hundred thousand times a RAM access, so once the active working set exceeds physical memory the fault rate, not the total size, decides performance.

Now apply it where it is less obvious: A batch job touches 8 GB sequentially once, on a 4 GB machine. Say whether it will thrash and why the access pattern matters.

The browser is a convenience, not a boundary. Client-side validation exists for speed of feedback; the trust boundary is the server, which receives requests from anything that can speak HTTP. So every constraint that matters - type, range, ownership, permission - must be enforced server-side, ideally with database constraints behind it as the last line. The rule generalises: never trust anything that crossed the network, including hidden fields, prices and identifiers you put there yourself.

What your sentence leaves implicit: Validate on the server for every request as the authoritative check, and keep the client checks purely as fast feedback. Your page is not the only client: a request tool can post any payload to the same endpoint, so anything only the browser enforces is not enforced at all.

Try 12 on the Web Application Development exercise about HTTP statelessness and sessions. What I have so far: HTTP is a stateless protocol. Just tell me the answer?

Right: no more questions, here is the answer with the reasoning attached.

HTTP requests are independent; the server keeps no thread between them by itself. A session is built by issuing a random, unguessable token at login, storing it in a cookie, and having the browser send it with every subsequent request so the server can look up the session record. That design has direct consequences: the token must be random (not a user id), marked HttpOnly and Secure, rotated at login, and expired server-side - because whoever holds it is the session.
Okay. So was after login the server knows who the user is, so the later requests do not need to send anything extra completely wrong, or just incomplete?

Incomplete rather than random - it is a reasonable reading of the evidence you had. The specific thing that makes it fail: Each request is a fresh conversation, so identity has to be re-established per request - the cookie is the only thread connecting them, which is also why stealing it is equivalent to stealing the session.

Start from what the record commits you to. [lecture#web-w7-state] says: Week 7: sessions must use a random server-side token; the assignment marks cookie attributes. That sentence is the standard your answer will be marked against, so everything below serves it.

HTTP requests are independent; the server keeps no thread between them by itself. A session is built by issuing a random, unguessable token at login, storing it in a cookie, and having the browser send it with every subsequent request so the server can look up the session record. That design has direct consequences: the token must be random (not a user id), marked HttpOnly and Secure, rotated at login, and expired server-side - because whoever holds it is the session.

Before I go further - The user loads three pages after logging in. What, in each of those three requests, tells the server who they are?
I think the answer is that each request arrives independently with no memory of the last one.

What your sentence leaves implicit: Send an unguessable session token on every request and resolve identity server-side from that token, rather than assuming continuity. Each request is a fresh conversation, so identity has to be re-established per request - the cookie is the only thread connecting them, which is also why stealing it is equivalent to stealing the session.

The same-origin policy is a browser rule: scripts on origin A may send a request to origin B but may not read the response unless B opts in. CORS is that opt-in - response headers naming the permitted origin, methods and headers, with a preflight OPTIONS for anything non-simple. Two consequences: a CORS failure is not the server rejecting you (curl still works), and CORS is not access control - it protects users' browsers, not your API, which still needs authentication.

Question: I answered this in the Mobile Computing quiz and got it back with no comments. Set out battery and background work and the condition where it breaks. What would a marker say?

Student answer: Waking the cellular radio is far more expensive than the computation itself. each wake-up has a tail cost, so batching saves power. the operating system batches and delays background jobs to protect battery. use the platform's job scheduler with constraints instead of a timer that fires every minute.

Official rubric points:
1. Says radio use dominates battery cost
2. Says frequent small syncs are worse than batched ones
3. Says the platform defers background work deliberately
4. Names a correct API-level approach

Verdict: correct - 4 of 4 points, and the reasoning is yours.

- Point 1 (Says radio use dominates battery cost): "waking the cellular radio is far more expensive than the computation itself"
- Point 2 (Says frequent small syncs are worse than batched ones): "each wake-up has a tail cost, so batching saves power"
- Point 3 (Says the platform defers background work deliberately): "the operating system batches and delays background jobs to protect battery"
- Point 4 (Names a correct API-level approach): "use the platform's job scheduler with constraints instead of a timer that fires every minute"

The next level of this: you have the rule; the place people lose it later is under pressure, when that battery cost tracks how much code you run, so a small periodic task must be cheap creeps back in. Your answer already rules that out, so keep the sentence that does it.

COD answers a trust problem - the buyer does not have to trust the seller or the payment channel - and it does so by moving risk onto the seller, who ships and pays for delivery before receiving anything. Mitigations are verification before dispatch (a call or one-time code), partial prepayment of the delivery fee, refusal-rate tracking by area, and giving buyers a reason to prepay, such as a small discount that is cheaper than the refusal loss.

COD answers a trust problem - the buyer does not have to trust the seller or the payment channel - and it does so by moving risk onto the seller, who ships and pays for delivery before receiving anything. The failure modes are refusal at the door, false addresses, cash handling and slower cash conversion. Mitigations are verification before dispatch (a call or one-time code), partial prepayment of the delivery fee, refusal-rate tracking by area, and giving buyers a reason to prepay, such as a small discount that is cheaper than the refusal loss.

Lossless coding removes redundancy and can reconstruct every original bit. Lossy coding removes information, chosen with a perceptual model - fine chroma detail, frequencies near the masking threshold - and that information is not in the file afterwards. The working rule is to keep a lossless or original master and export derivatives from it every time.

Raster stores a sampled grid: quality is bounded by the samples you captured, and enlarging interpolates. Vector stores geometry - paths, fills, control points - which is rendered at whatever resolution the output needs, so it scales cleanly. That makes vector right for logos, type and diagrams, and raster right for photographs, which are samples of continuous tone with no underlying shapes. Auto-tracing a photograph converts noise into thousands of flat polygons: a bigger file, no new detail.

Two independent axes. Sample rate sets the frequency ceiling: by Nyquist you can represent components below half the rate, so 8 kHz keeps under 4 kHz - enough for intelligible speech, not for the sibilance that reads as clarity. Bit depth sets amplitude resolution and the noise floor. Neither can be recovered after capture: upsampling interpolates between existing samples and adds no new frequency content. Git is a distributed version control system: your clone contains the full history, so commit, log, diff, branch, merge and revert are local and work with no connection. 1. Says you collect only what the purpose requires
2. Says the purpose must be stated and limited
3. Says retention must be bounded
4. Says identifiers raise the stakes

- Point 3 (Says retention must be bounded): "delete the data once the purpose has been served"
- Point 4 (Says identifiers raise the stakes): "storing a national id or phone number makes a breach far more damaging"

Course: Computer Organization (week 2, topic: caches and locality, status: KNOWN).

Question: My tutor says my answer on caches and locality is not complete. Explain caches and locality and say what actually decides the outcome. Which points am I losing and why?

Student answer: The cache keeps recently used data in fast memory near the processor. programs reuse the same data soon, and use neighbouring addresses soon. a miss fetches a whole line, so neighbouring values arrive too. iterating along rows matches the layout and hits cache, iterating down columns does not.

Official rubric points:
1. Says a cache holds recently used data closer to the CPU
2. Names temporal and spatial locality
3. Says data moves in cache lines, not single bytes
4. Connects access pattern to performance

Verdict: correct. All 4 points are there, so this is a submission-quality answer.

Earned, with the words that earned them:
- Point 1 (Says a cache holds recently used data closer to the CPU): "the cache keeps recently used data in fast memory near the processor"
- Point 2 (Names temporal and spatial locality): "programs reuse the same data soon, and use neighbouring addresses soon"
- Point 3 (Says data moves in cache lines, not single bytes): "a miss fetches a whole line, so neighbouring values arrive too"
- Point 4 (Connects access pattern to performance): "iterating along rows matches the layout and hits cache, iterating down columns does not"

Where this answer could still be sharpened: you have the rule; the place people lose it later is under pressure, when that memory access cost is uniform, so two loops doing the same number of operations must take the same time creeps back in. Your answer already rules that out, so keep the sentence that does it.

Do this next: You must sum a column of a large row-major matrix many times. Propose a change to the data layout and say what it costs elsewhere.

Question: What is the one thing I have to understand about caches and locality?

Start from what the record commits you to. [lecture#co-w7-memory] says: Week 7: performance claims must reference the cache line and the access stride. That sentence is the standard your answer will be marked against, so everything below serves it.

Memory is a hierarchy, and a miss costs on the order of a hundred times a hit. Hardware exploits locality: it fetches a whole cache line (typically 64 bytes) and prefetches predictable strides. A row-major array places row neighbours adjacently, so row-order iteration uses every byte of each fetched line while column-order iteration uses one value per line and evicts it before returning. Same operation count, very different miss count - which is why layout and traversal order are performance decisions.

Before I go further - Your inner loop jumps 2,000 elements each step. How much of the line the hardware just fetched do you use?
I think the answer is that the cache keeps recently used data in fast memory near the processor.

Yes - that is the load-bearing half, and you got to it from the record rather than from memory, which is the habit that scores.

What your sentence leaves implicit: Order the loops to match the memory layout, because a miss brings in a whole cache line and the next elements of a row are already in it. Each miss fetches a line of neighbouring bytes, so a stride that skips a full row wastes most of every fetched line and multiplies misses.

Now apply it where it is less obvious: You must sum a column of a large row-major matrix many times. Propose a change to the data layout and say what it costs elsewhere.

Our CI is cursed. Since we enabled parallel test execution, builds fail 'randomly' — different tests each time. Re-running usually goes green, so we just re-run until it passes. But here's the weird part I found today: test_apply_discount PASSES in the full suite run but FAILS when I run it alone. A test that only passes with company! It hides it, which is different — and your 'weird part' is actually the confession. Think about what a test that passes WITH company but fails ALONE is telling you. For test_apply_discount to behave differently depending on which tests ran before it, something must persist from those earlier tests into its world. What does that imply about the world your tests run in?

They're sharing something. Each test isn't getting a fresh world — some earlier test leaves state behind that test_apply_discount silently depends on. Run alone, the state is missing, so it fails. So it's not testing my discount code at all — it's testing 'my discount code, given whatever test_create_user happened to leave lying around'. Let me look... oh. There's a module-level price cache that test_load_catalog populates, and test_apply_discount reads it. And they both hit the same seeded database rows, which test_update_prices MODIFIES.

Two smoking guns, one crime: shared mutable state — a module-level cache and shared database rows — turning your 'independent' tests into an accidental pipeline where order is load-bearing. Now explain your own CI mystery with this: why did everything SEEM fine before parallelism, and why do different tests fail each run now?

Sequential execution always ran tests in the same order, so the hidden dependencies were always satisfied by accident — the pipeline worked because it always ran in pipeline order. Parallelism shuffles and interleaves: sometimes test_apply_discount runs before test_load_catalog populated the cache, sometimes test_update_prices clobbers rows mid-flight in another worker. Which test fails depends on the interleaving of that particular run — that's the 'randomness'. It's the same disease as the race conditions from OS class, except my tests are the threads and my fixtures are the shared memory!

Exactly the same disease — and parallelism didn't cause it, it EXPOSED coupling that was already lying to you sequentially: any test passing because of a predecessor's leftovers isn't verifying what its name claims. Which brings me to the habit I most want to take away from you: re-running until green. Walk through what that policy does to the INFORMATION your test suite produces.

My class project charged a test user twice and I can't see how. My client code: send `POST /charge {user, amount}`; if the request times out after 3 seconds, retry, up to 3 attempts. That's just standard robust networking — retrying failed requests is what you're SUPPOSED to do. The duplicate has to be a bug in the payments library, right?

Before blaming the library, interrogate one word in your description: you said 'retrying *failed* requests.' Your code retries on timeout. Are those the same thing?

Be precise: a timeout means 3 seconds passed with no response. Enumerate every state the *server* could be in at that moment. There are more than one.

States... one: my request never arrived — network ate it, server did nothing. Two: server got it, is just slow, still processing. Three: server got it, processed it, CHARGED the card... and the response got lost or delayed on the way back. Oh. The timeout can't tell me which. In state one, retrying is correct and safe. In state three, retrying charges them again. My retry logic isn't wrong because retrying is bad — it's wrong because a timeout isn't a failure, it's an *unknown outcome*, and I coded it as if it were a known failure.

That reclassification — timeout as unknown, not failure — is the entire discipline of this bug, and notice the library is now exonerated: it did exactly what it was asked, twice. Here's the trap fully sprung: you cannot distinguish those states from the client (that's fundamental — the response that would tell you is exactly what's missing), and NOT retrying is also wrong, because state one is common and users hate dead payment buttons.

So the requirements are: you must retry, AND retrying after a completed charge must not charge again. You can change the server. Design it: what would the server need in order to recognize 'I have already done this exact operation' when the retry arrives — and be careful, 'same user, same amount' won't work. Why not?

My C++ assignment: two threads each increment a shared `int counter` 100,000 times. Final value should be 200,000 but I get random junk like 137482, different every run. `counter++` is ONE statement — one line of code! How can half a statement execute? Is the thread scheduler broken on my laptop?

Your laptop is fine, and the phrase to interrogate is 'one statement.' One line of C++ is not one machine action. Before any concurrency talk: what must the CPU actually do, at the register level, to add 1 to a variable that lives in memory? Break `counter++` into its smallest steps — there are three.

Load counter from memory into a register, add 1 to the register, store the register back to memory. Okay, three steps, but so what? Each thread still does all three steps every time — nothing gets skipped, so the count should still come out right.

'Nothing gets skipped' is true — and yet updates vanish. So the loss must come from *ordering*, not omission. Time for you to be the scheduler, with full sadistic freedom to pause a thread between ANY two of its steps.

Let me try... A loads 500. Pause A. B loads 500 — it can't see A's plan, A hasn't stored yet. B adds, B stores 501. Resume A: A adds to ITS register copy — 501 — and stores 501. Both finished honestly, but B's increment got overwritten like it never happened. A stored a value computed from stale data... so with 100,000 iterations this collision happens thousands of times, and every collision eats an update. That's why my number is different every run — it depends on where the scheduler happened to slice.

You just constructed a *lost update* — and more importantly, you've located the disease precisely: the load-modify-store sequence must be indivisible, or two threads can both compute from the same stale snapshot.

Atomic is cheaper — it's a single hardware instruction, no lock overhead, no thread ever sleeps. But it only protects ONE operation on ONE object. If three variables must change together as a unit, atomics on each don't help — another thread could see one updated and two stale. The mutex buys me an indivisible REGION of arbitrary code, not just an indivisible instruction.

Instruction-level versus region-level indivisibility — that distinction will carry you through the rest of this course. Final challenge before you write it up: your fixed program prints 200,000 every time now, but run it with the mutex version and time it against the single-threaded loop. You may find the 'parallel' version *slower*.

This is breaking my brain. User 'José' registered on his phone, then can't log in from the lab PC. I printed the stored username and the typed one: both show José. IDENTICAL. But == says false! I even checked the lengths — stored is 5 characters, typed is 4. HOW can the same four visible letters have different lengths? Is the database corrupting my strings?

You've already collected the killer clue and walked past it: same visible text, DIFFERENT lengths. Corruption produces garbage; yours produced a perfectly readable name with one extra invisible something. So stop looking at the rendered glyphs — they're the wrong witness. Print the actual code points of each string, one per line, in hex. What do you see around the é?

Whoa. Typed version: J, o, s, U+00E9 — four code points, that last one is 'LATIN SMALL LETTER E WITH ACUTE'. Stored version: J, o, s, U+0065, U+0301 — FIVE code points: a plain 'e' followed by 'COMBINING ACUTE ACCENT'. So there are two completely different ways to spell é?! One ready-made character, and one built from an e plus a floating accent that renders on top of it?

Both fully legal, both rendering identically — Unicode calls them canonically equivalent: different code point sequences, same abstract character. The precomposed form (U+00E9) exists for compatibility with older encodings; the combining form (e + U+0301) is the general mechanism — some scripts stack several marks, and you can't precompose every combination. Now the diagnostic question: same user, same name — why did his PHONE produce one form and the LAB PC the other?

Different input systems make different choices — the phone keyboard emits precomposed characters, but maybe the lab PC's input method, or whatever the registration website's framework did, produced the decomposed form. So my strings aren't corrupted anywhere; they were BORN different at two different keyboards, and my == is doing exactly what it promises: comparing code point sequences, which really are different. The bug is that I treated 'same code points' and 'same text' as the same question.

That last sentence is the entire field of Unicode handling. Equality of SEQUENCES is what the machine gives you; equality of TEXT is what the human means; and Unicode provides the bridge — normalization. The standard defines transformations to a canonical form: NFC (compose everything precomposable — José becomes 4 code points) and NFD (decompose everything — 5 code points). Normalize both strings to the SAME form, then compare.

My crawler needs to answer 'have I seen this URL before?' for a billion URLs. A hash set of them is 60+ gigabytes — I have 6. Facts are facts: to know if a URL is in the set, the set has to contain the URL. So I need 10 machines I don't have, or I crawl duplicates and waste half my bandwidth. Compression buys you maybe 2-3x; you need 10x, so let's attack the assumption instead: 'to know membership, you must store the elements.' That's true for EXACT answers. But interrogate your actual requirement — in your crawler, what happens on each kind of wrong answer? Case one: the filter says 'seen it' about a URL you actually haven't visited. Case two: it says 'never seen it' about one you have. Walk through the consequences of each.

Case two is poison: 'never seen it' for a visited URL means I re-crawl it — and worse, if it happens systematically I could loop forever on the same pages. Case one though... 'seen it' for a fresh URL just means I SKIP one page I've never visited. I lose a tiny bit of coverage. If that happened to, say, 1% of new URLs, I'd barely notice — the web has a billion more pages. Huh. The two error directions have wildly different prices. So if some structure could promise 'no false negatives, ever' and 'false positives, rarely'... I could pay 1% coverage for a 10x memory win?

That asymmetric deal exists, and you're going to build it. Start tiny: instead of storing URLs, take a bit array of m bits, all zero, and one hash function. To ADD a URL: hash it to a position, set that bit to 1. To QUERY: hash, check the bit. Analyze: which error direction can this make, and which can it never make?

I think this API is broken. My code:

```js
let data;
fetch('/api/courses')
  .then(res => res.json())
  .then(json => { data = json; });
console.log(data); // undefined!!
```

I can literally SEE the request succeed with a 200 in the network tab, and `data = json` definitely runs because a log inside there prints the courses. But the outer console.log prints undefined. How is that possible if the request works?

The API is innocent — and your two observations ('the inner log prints data' but 'the outer log prints undefined') are actually the complete evidence. They just happen in a different ORDER than the source code reads.

Do this: put `console.log('A')` inside your second `.then`, and `console.log('B')` on the outer console.log line. Run it. Which letter prints first?
B prints first?! But B is written BELOW the fetch. How does JavaScript run my code out of order?

It doesn't run out of order — it runs in two waves, and that's the mental model shift.

Wave 1: JavaScript executes your script top to bottom WITHOUT stopping. `fetch(...)` doesn't perform the download right there — it only *starts* it and registers your `.then` callbacks as 'call these later, when the response lands.' Then it keeps going and runs your outer `console.log(data)` — at which point `data` was never assigned. That's B.

Wave 2: milliseconds later the response arrives, and only now do your `.then` callbacks run. That's A, and that's when `data` finally gets its value — too late for B.
Inside the .then chain... or somewhere that runs during Wave 2. So I should move my rendering code into the .then instead of trying to smuggle data out into a global variable?

Exactly — 'smuggling data out to the top level' is the anti-pattern, and you named it yourself. Code that depends on the response belongs downstream of the response: inside the `.then`, or in a function the `.then` calls.

Restructure it that way and run it. Then, one more experiment so this generalizes: wrap the same logic in an `async` function using `await fetch(...)` and log your A/B letters again. You'll see `await` doesn't break the two-wave model — it's syntax that lets you write Wave 2 code so it *reads* like Wave 1. Tell me what order you get.

Our capstone team is turning our project into an actual startup — closed source, paid product. We use a GPL-licensed PDF library at the core of it. A classmate said we 'can't do that' but that makes no sense: the code is publicly on GitHub, free to download, no password, nothing. If they didn't want people using it, why publish it? Free is free, right?

You're conflating two different 'free's, and the gap between them is exactly where startups get hurt. Publicly downloadable means free of CHARGE. The license governs free of OBLIGATION — and GPL charges a price that isn't money. Go to the library's LICENSE file, find the section about 'conveying' a work based on the program, and tell me what it demands from YOUR product in exchange for using theirs.

...Section 5: if we distribute a work based on this library, we must license OUR ENTIRE WORK under the GPL too, and provide the source code. Wait — so the price of using their free library is making our whole closed-source product open source?! That's the opposite of our business model. Why would anyone design a license that... infects the host program like that?

'Infects' is the hostile framing; understand the author's intent and the design becomes rational. GPL authors are making a deal: 'I give you my work; in exchange, whatever you build on it stays free for the NEXT person, forever.' The copyleft clause is the enforcement mechanism — without it, companies could take community code proprietary and give nothing back. It's not a trap; it's a value system with legal teeth, and the author chose it deliberately.

Option one: take the deal — open-source our product (kills our model). Option two: replace the library with one under a permissive license... MIT or Apache, which basically just want attribution? Option three: check if the GPL library's authors sell a commercial license separately — I've seen 'dual licensing' on some projects. And I guess option zero we've been doing — ignore it — is the one that ends with lawyers.

All four correctly priced — and dual licensing is exactly how many GPL projects fund themselves, so option three is a real email worth sending. One nuance to check before you rip anything out: LGPL (Lesser GPL) permits dynamic LINKING from proprietary code — if your PDF library is actually LGPL, your architecture might already be compliant. Read the actual license name character by character; GPL vs LGPL vs AGPL are different deals.

I think the filesystem is corrupted. The disk hit 100%, I found the culprit — a 30GB app.log — and deleted it with rm. It's GONE, ls shows nothing. But df STILL says 100% full! And here's the crazy part: du on the whole disk adds up to 30GB LESS than what df reports used. The numbers don't agree with each other. Before I reformat, is there any way to fix a filesystem this broken?

Do not reformat — your filesystem isn't broken, and the 30GB disagreement between du and df is not noise; it's a precise clue, because those two tools count DIFFERENT things. du walks the directory tree adding up files it can reach by name. df asks the filesystem how many blocks are allocated, reachable or not.

I assumed rm deletes the file — data and all. But given the evidence... it removed the NAME, the directory entry, and the data blocks are somehow still allocated. Is that why the syscall is called unlink and not delete? Like the name is just a link to the actual file?

You've just read a decades-old design decision straight out of a syscall name — yes. In Unix filesystems, a file IS an inode: the data blocks plus metadata, identified by number. A directory entry is merely a name pointing at an inode, and one inode can have many names (hard links).

An open file descriptor! The app that WRITES app.log — it's still running, and it opened that log file ages ago. It doesn't care about the name; it holds a handle straight to the inode. So the kernel keeps the inode alive because the process might still read or write it... and in fact my app is probably STILL WRITING to the deleted file right now, growing those invisible 30GB even bigger. That's why the disk stays full!

Exactly — the inode's lifetime is governed by a reference count: link count (names) plus open handles, and the blocks free only when BOTH hit zero. Your rm took the link count to zero, but one open handle keeps the corpse warm — and yes, still growing.

The blunt way: restart the app — the handle closes on exit, references hit zero, 30GB frees instantly. Gentler... could I empty the file through the handle instead of removing it? Like truncate the still-open file to zero bytes? If the app has the file open, there must be a path to it through the process — /proc maybe?

Both correct, and the second is the professional's move: `truncate -s 0 /proc/PID/fd/N` — or better, BEFORE deleting next time, `truncate -s 0 app.log` or `> app.log`, which empties the data while keeping the same inode, so the app's handle stays valid and the space frees immediately.

My client-server protocol is crawling and the number is WEIRD. Localhost, tiny messages, and every request-response takes almost exactly 40ms. Not 38, not 45 — it's like a metronome. Real network latency is noisy; this is too consistent. Is the OS throttling my socket? I send the 4-byte header first, then the payload, then wait for the response.

Your instinct about the number is superb and it's the whole case: noisy causes make noisy delays, so a metronomic 40ms means you're hitting a configured TIMER, not congestion or throttling. Something in the stack is deliberately waiting for a timeout that's set to tens of milliseconds.

One character = 1 byte of payload wrapped in 40 bytes of headers — 4000% overhead, and thousands of tiny packets flooding the network. So TCP probably... batches? Waits a bit to see if more bytes are coming before sending a packet?

Exactly — that's Nagle's algorithm, and its rule is elegant: you may have at most ONE small unacknowledged packet in flight; further small writes get buffered until either you've got a full packet's worth, or the outstanding packet's ACK comes back.

Nagle says: there's already one small unACKed packet in flight (the header), so the payload BUFFERS until the header's ACK arrives. Fine, the ACK should come instantly... but the server's delayed-ACK timer says: 'don't ACK yet — wait, data will probably come back to piggyback on.' And the server's application CAN'T respond with data, because it only has my header — it needs the payload to process the request, and the payload is stuck in my client's buffer waiting for the very ACK the server is withholding! They're waiting for each other. The deadlock only breaks when the server's 40ms timer expires and it grudgingly sends the bare ACK. THAT'S my metronome.

You've just traced one of the most famous performance interactions in networking — and notice the philosophical shape of what you found, because it recurs everywhere in systems: Nagle is CORRECT in isolation, delayed ACK is CORRECT in isolation, and their composition produces a 40ms livelock that n

Fix one: stop doing write-write-read. Build the header and payload into ONE buffer, one write() call — then it's a single packet, no small-packet-in-flight rule triggered, no waiting. Fix two: the socket option that turns Nagle off — TCP_NODELAY, right? Then every write goes out immediately regardless. Honestly fix two sounds easier, just set the flag everywhere.
It IS easier, which is why half the internet's application code sets it reflexively — but 'set it everywhere' is a scalpel used as a policy, so make the choice like an engineer.

I caught the textbook lying. It says dynamic array append is O(1). So I benchmarked a million appends and timed EACH one. Most are nanoseconds, fine — but every so often one append takes THOUSANDS of times longer. Append number 524,289 was a monster. That's not O(1), that's O(n) sometimes! Why does the textbook teach something my own measurements disprove?

Your benchmark is correct, your reading of it is correct, and the textbook is ALSO correct — which means the interesting thing here is the word that reconciles them, and you're about to derive it. First, your monster: append 524,289. That number is 2^19 + 1.

Powers of two... the array's capacity doubles when it fills! It had capacity 524,288, my append didn't fit, so it allocated a new array of 1,048,576 and copied every existing element over — half a million copies inside one 'append'. That's the spike. So SOME appends genuinely cost O(n). Which is my point — the claim 'O(1)' is false!

For that individual append, you're right — it cost O(n), no defense. But now do the accounting question the textbook is actually answering: not 'what does the worst single append cost' but 'what do n appends cost IN TOTAL'. Add up the copying across your whole million-append run.

1 + 2 + 4 + ... + 524,288. Geometric series — that sums to just under 2 × 524,288, about 1,048,575. So a million appends did about a million copies TOTAL, plus the million cheap writes themselves. Total work ≈ 2 million operations for 1 million appends... which is 2 operations per append. Oh. The spikes are huge but so RARE that they average out to a constant. The expensive copies at size 2^k are paid for by the 2^k cheap appends that preceded them.

You've just performed amortized analysis — that's the reconciling word. The claim is 'append is amortized O(1)': any sequence of n appends costs O(n) total, so per-operation cost, averaged over the SEQUENCE, is constant — even though individual operations spike.

Copies happen at 1000, 2000, 3000, ... so for n appends there are n/1000 resizes, copying 1000 + 2000 + ... + n elements — that's an arithmetic series, about n²/2000 total copies. Quadratic! A million appends would do five hundred million copies instead of one million. So growing by a constant makes append amortized O(n) per operation, not O(1). The DOUBLING is what makes the geometric series converge... the growth has to be multiplicative. That's actually a huge difference from what looks like a minor tuning choice.

That contrast is the entire reason amortized analysis exists as a tool: it's the only lens that distinguishes doubling from +1000 — both look identical in a casual glance at the code, both have the same worst-case single append, and one of them quietly turns your program quadratic.

This is breaking my brain. User 'José' registered on his phone, then can't log in from the lab PC. I printed the stored username and the typed one: both show José. IDENTICAL. But == says false! I even checked the lengths — stored is 5 characters, typed is 4. HOW can the same four visible letters have different lengths? Is the database corrupting my strings?

You've already collected the killer clue and walked past it: same visible text, DIFFERENT lengths. Corruption produces garbage; yours produced a perfectly readable name with one extra invisible something. So stop looking at the rendered glyphs — they're the wrong witness.

Whoa. Typed version: J, o, s, U+00E9 — four code points, that last one is 'LATIN SMALL LETTER E WITH ACUTE'. Stored version: J, o, s, U+0065, U+0301 — FIVE code points: a plain 'e' followed by 'COMBINING ACUTE ACCENT'. So there are two completely different ways to spell é?! One ready-made character, and one built from an e plus a floating accent that renders on top of it?

Both fully legal, both rendering identically — Unicode calls them canonically equivalent: different code point sequences, same abstract character. The precomposed form (U+00E9) exists for compatibility with older encodings; the combining form (e + U+0301) is the general mechanism

Different input systems make different choices — the phone keyboard emits precomposed characters, but maybe the lab PC's input method, or whatever the registration website's framework did, produced the decomposed form. So my strings aren't corrupted anywhere; they were BORN different at two different keyboards, and my == is doing exactly what it promises: comparing code point sequences, which really are different. The bug is that I treated 'same code points' and 'same text' as the same question.

That last sentence is the entire field of Unicode handling. Equality of SEQUENCES is what the machine gives you; equality of TEXT is what the human means; and Unicode provides the bridge — normalization.

If I only normalize when comparing, every other operation stays broken — the database unique-index would still allow both 'José's to register as different users, searches would miss, sorting would split them... I should normalize at the BOUNDARY: the moment text enters my system — form input, API, file import — convert to NFC once, store only NFC, and then everything downstream can use plain == safely. One choke point instead of a hundred defensive comparisons.

Normalize-at-ingest is exactly the professional pattern, and NFC is the right default (it's what the W3C recommends for the web, and most wire text already arrives that way). Three closing items to make this stick.

I've spent three days hunting a duplicate-rows bug that doesn't exist. Users swear items show up at the bottom of page 1 AND the top of page 2, and other items never show up at all. But I've queried the table directly — no duplicate rows, no missing rows, data is perfect! My endpoint is just SELECT * FROM activities ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 20*(page-1). The data is clean, the query is textbook... is the driver duplicating rows in transit?

Your data is clean and your query is textbook — and both facts survive while the users are ALSO right. Here's the reframe that dissolves the paradox: the users aren't making one query; they're making a SEQUENCE of queries with time gaps between them, against a table that's alive. Simulate it by hand with a 5-row table, page size 2, newest first.

Page 1: newest two — E, D. Then F inserts at the top, so the order is now F E D C B A. Page 2 says 'skip 2, take 2': skips F and E... returns D, C. D AGAIN — the user just saw D at the bottom of page 1! The insert shifted every existing row down one position, so the skip-counter skips F (never seen) and E (seen), and re-serves D. And it's worse in the other direction: if rows got DELETED between clicks, everything shifts UP and the skip-counter would jump OVER a row the user never saw. Duplicates from inserts, gaps from deletes — and my feed has constant inserts. There is no bug in the data. OFFSET is counting from a moving edge.

'Counting from a moving edge' — that's the whole disease in five words. OFFSET doesn't identify rows; it counts positions from the top, and the top of a newest-first live feed is precisely the most unstable location in the entire table. So: design the cure. The user's real request isn't 'rows at positions 21-40' — nobody thinks in positions.

'Show me what comes AFTER the last thing I saw.' The anchor should be the CONTENT, not the position — the query should be WHERE created_at < [D's timestamp] ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20. Then new inserts at the top can't shift anything: D's timestamp is a fixed point, and 'older than D' is stable no matter what arrives above. The API returns each page plus a cursor — the last row's timestamp — and the client sends it back for the next page. Wait, one hole: what if two activities share the exact same timestamp? The boundary would be ambiguous — I could still skip or duplicate WITHIN a timestamp tie.

Catching the tie-break hole yourself puts you ahead of half the production implementations out there. The standard fix: a compound cursor — ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC with WHERE (created_at, id) < (:ts, :id). The id disambiguates ties, and since it's unique, every boundary is exact.

But the same comparison on a string the user typed in comes back false even when I can PRINT both strings and see they're identical. Same operator, same-looking strings, different results. The cruelest part of your situation is the 'sometimes it works' — if `==` failed every time, you'd have fixed this in five minutes. So let's explain both halves: why it fails, and — the half that actually matters — why it ever succeeded.

First half. In Java, a `String` variable doesn't hold the text; it holds a *reference* — an arrow pointing at a String object in memory. So spell out what question `a == b` is actually asking in Java. Is it about the text?

If they're arrows, then `==` compares the arrows — 'do these point at the SAME object?' — not the letters. Two separate String objects could both contain 'go' and `==` would say false because they're two boxes at two addresses. Fine, that explains the user-input failure. But then my test should ALSO have failed! `a` and `b` were two separate variables — why did `==` say true for my two literals?

That's the right question, and its answer is the trap's engine. When the compiler sees the *literal* "go" written twice in your source code, it plays a memory-saving trick called **interning**: identical compile-time literals are folded into ONE shared object in a string pool. So `a` and `b` are two arrows pointing at the same pooled object — `==` honestly answers 'same object? yes.' Your test accidentally asked the one question where arrow-equality and text-equality coincide.

User input, file reads, string concatenation at runtime — those build *fresh* objects at runtime; the pool trick doesn't apply. Now diagnose yourself like a doctor would: which Python fact did you import as if it were universal, and what made Python safe for that habit?

My DNS update half-worked and I don't know how to fix it. I changed the A record to the new server's IP two hours ago. My phone gets the NEW site, the lab PC gets the OLD one, and my friend in London gets the new one. So the update reached some parts of the internet and failed to reach others? Should I delete and re-add the record to force it to push out again?

Before you touch that record again — your mental model has DNS as a broadcast system: you publish, the update gets PUSHED across the internet, and pushes can fail partway. Let's test that model against a scale question. There are billions of devices and millions of resolvers.

Pushing to millions of resolvers per change would be insane — the system would drown. And no, DNS is pull-based: a resolver ASKS the hierarchy when it needs a name. So... nothing is pushed anywhere, ever. My update didn't 'travel'. It just sits on the authoritative server waiting to be asked. But then why does the lab PC still get the OLD IP? If it asked right now, it'd get the new one... unless it's not asking. It's remembering.

'It's remembering' — now you have the real system. Every resolver in the chain — your OS, your router, your ISP's resolver — caches answers, because asking the hierarchy for google.com on every packet would be absurd.

TTL: 86400. That's seconds... 24 hours! So every resolver that asked about my domain in the last day is allowed to keep serving the OLD IP from cache for up to 24 hours from when it asked. My phone sees the new site because its cache happened to expire — or it never cached — while the lab PC's resolver cached the old answer recently and won't re-ask until its timer runs out. Nothing failed. Nothing is 'propagating'. A million independent caches are just expiring on a million independent schedules. That's why it looks random across devices!

Exactly — 'DNS propagation' is one of networking's great misnomers: nothing propagates; caches expire, each on its own clock, and the messy in-between period is that expiry happening unevenly. Your 'half-failed update' is the system working precisely as designed.

Lower the TTL in advance! Like: a day or two BEFORE the migration, change TTL from 86400 to 300 seconds — then wait out the old 24h TTL so all caches pick up the short one. Now every cache re-asks every 5 minutes. Do the IP switch: worst case, anyone is stale for 5 minutes. Then once it's verified, raise the TTL back up so caches aren't hammering my server forever. The migration playbook is: shrink the memory window first, move, then relax it again.

That's the professional playbook to the letter — including the step people forget: you must lower the TTL at least one OLD-TTL-length before the move, because caches holding the 24-hour answer won't see your new 5-minute TTL until they next expire.

Git has lost its mind. I rebased our develop branch last night to squash the ugly 'wip' commits into clean ones — looked beautiful — and force-pushed. This morning both teammates get 'your branch and origin have diverged', Kwesi's pull created a pile of duplicate commits, and Abena says her yesterday's work is GONE from origin. Nothing corrupted, and we'll get Abena's work back — recovery first, understanding second. Abena's commits almost certainly still exist on her LOCAL machine (tell her: `git reflog` will show them even if her branch pointer moved; and they may exist on the remote's reflog too, plus your own pre-rebase state is in YOUR reflog). Have her run reflog and find yesterday's commit hashes NOW, before any 'cleanup' makes it harder. Done? Good.

I thought it kind of... reshuffled them? But commits are content-addressed — the hash covers the content AND the parent pointers — so you can't edit one in place; changing anything makes a DIFFERENT commit with a different hash. So my rebase built a parallel set of brand-new commits with new hashes and moved the branch label to point at them. The old commits didn't get edited... they got replaced and abandoned. Oh. And everything my teammates did yesterday has parent pointers into the ABANDONED line.

There it is. Your teammates' local work is built on ancestors that origin/develop no longer acknowledges — their commits are grandchildren of ghosts. That's exactly the two symptoms: 'diverged' (their line and your new line share no recent history), and Kwesi's duplicates (his pull tried to merge the ghost line with your replacement line — same changes, different hashes, so git treats them as unrelated commits that happen to collide).

The force-push. Rebasing MY OWN unpushed commits hurts nobody — I'm replacing history only I have seen; nothing is built on it. The crime was replacing history other people had already pulled and built on. Force-push was me overwriting the shared record and everyone else's work still referenced the old one. So the rule is something like: rewrite private history freely, never rewrite published history?

That's the rule, verbatim: **history you've shared is a contract; history you haven't is a draft.** Squash and reorder your drafts all you like — it's actively good practice before opening a PR. Published history gets fixed FORWARD: `git revert` creates new commits that undo old ones, correcting the record without rewriting it.

This makes no sense. My robot's control loop is priority 10, the HIGHEST. I raised it there specifically so nothing could delay it. But it still misses deadlines, and the log is insane: my priority-10 control task sits BLOCKED for 300ms while a priority-5 telemetry task runs the whole time. The scheduler is broken — priority 10 should always beat priority 5!

Your log isn't insane — it's showing you a genuinely famous phenomenon, and you have all the pieces to reconstruct it. Start here: the scheduler only runs tasks that are RUNNABLE. Your control task is 'blocked', you said. A priority-10 task doesn't block because a priority-5 task exists — priorities can't block anyone. What KINDS of things make a task block, regardless of its priority?

Waiting for I/O... waiting on a timer... or waiting for a lock. Oh — the control task and the low-priority logging task share a mutex around the sensor data buffer. The log does show the control task blocked at `sensor_mutex.acquire()`. But the LOGGING task is priority 2 — if it holds the mutex, it should finish its tiny critical section instantly and release it. It's like ten lines of code.

'It should finish instantly' — under what condition? Walk the scheduler's logic: the priority-2 logger is inside the critical section, holding the mutex your priority-10 task needs. For the logger to finish those ten lines and release, the logger has to be RUNNING. Look at your log again: who is actually on the CPU during those 300ms?

The priority-5 telemetry task. It doesn't touch the mutex at all, it's just... runnable, and priority 5 beats priority 2. So the scheduler — correctly, by its own rules — runs telemetry instead of the logger. And the logger can't finish its ten lines because it never gets the CPU. And my priority-10 task can't run because it's blocked on the mutex the logger can't release. The MEDIUM task is effectively outranking my HIGHEST task, without ever touching anything my task needs. The priorities have... inverted.

You just coined the textbook term yourself: priority inversion. High waits on a lock held by Low; Low is starved by Medium; therefore Medium's runtime becomes High's delay — unbounded, because any number of medium tasks can pile in. Notice the trap you were in: you kept raising the control task's priority, but its priority was never the problem — a blocked task's priority is irrelevant, since blocked tasks aren't schedulable at any priority. So the fix has to act somewhere else.

I've been doing linear search on my own repo for three hours.

And because every engineer eventually has your exact three hours, git ships the algorithm as a first-class command: `git bisect`. You declare the endpoints — `git bisect start`, `git bisect bad HEAD`, `git bisect good v2.1` — and git checks out the midpoint. You run your tests, tell it `git bisect good` or `git bisect bad`, and it halves again. Eight rounds later it prints the exact first bad commit. But your test suite takes what, four minutes? I think the filesystem is corrupted. The disk hit 100%, I found the culprit — a 30GB app.log — and deleted it with rm. It's GONE, ls shows nothing. But df STILL says 100% full! And here's the crazy part: du on the whole disk adds up to 30GB LESS than what df reports used. The numbers don't agree with each other. Before I reformat, is there any way to fix a filesystem this broken?

Do not reformat — your filesystem isn't broken, and the 30GB disagreement between du and df is not noise; it's a precise clue, because those two tools count DIFFERENT things. du walks the directory tree adding up files it can reach by name. df asks the filesystem how many blocks are allocated, reachable or not. So a du/df gap of exactly your deleted file's size says: 30GB of blocks are allocated but no longer reachable by any name. Which raises the real question — what did rm actually remove: the file's data, or something else?

I assumed rm deletes the file — data and all. But given the evidence... it removed the NAME, the directory entry, and the data blocks are somehow still allocated. Is that why the syscall is called unlink and not delete? Like the name is just a link to the actual file?

You've just read a decades-old design decision straight out of a syscall name — yes. In Unix filesystems, a file IS an inode: the data blocks plus metadata, identified by number. A directory entry is merely a name pointing at an inode, and one inode can have many names (hard links). So the filesystem can't free an inode when A name disappears; it has to wait until nothing refers to it. Names are one kind of reference. Your evidence says something else is still referring to that inode after the last name died.

An open file descriptor! The app that WRITES app.log — it's still running, and it opened that log file ages ago. It doesn't care about the name; it holds a handle straight to the inode. So the kernel keeps the inode alive because the process might still read or write it... and in fact my app is probably STILL WRITING to the deleted file right now, growing those invisible 30GB even bigger. That's why the disk stays full!

Exactly — the inode's lifetime is governed by a reference count: link count (names) plus open handles, and the blocks free only when BOTH hit zero. Your rm took the link count to zero, but one open handle keeps the corpse warm — and yes, still growing. You can see the ghost directly: `lsof +L1` lists open files with zero links — you'll find your app holding a 30GB-and-counting deleted file. So now the operational question, and it's the one that matters at 100% disk: how do you actually free the space — and is there a way to do it WITHOUT killing the app mid-request?

Git has lost its mind. I rebased our develop branch last night to squash the ugly 'wip' commits into clean ones — looked beautiful — and force-pushed. This morning both teammates get 'your branch and origin have diverged', Kwesi's pull created a pile of duplicate commits, and Abena says her yesterday's work is GONE from origin. I didn't delete anything! Did the force-push corrupt the remote?

Nothing corrupted, and we'll get Abena's work back — recovery first, understanding second. Abena's commits almost certainly still exist on her LOCAL machine (tell her: `git reflog` will show them even if her branch pointer moved; and they may exist on the remote's reflog too, plus your own pre-rebase state is in YOUR reflog). Have her run reflog and find yesterday's commit hashes NOW, before any 'cleanup' makes it harder. Done? Good. Now the understanding, because you're about to see why your beautiful rebase was a demolition. What does rebase actually do to the commits it 'cleans up' — does it edit them in place?

I thought it kind of... reshuffled them? But commits are content-addressed — the hash covers the content AND the parent pointers — so you can't edit one in place; changing anything makes a DIFFERENT commit with a different hash. So my rebase built a parallel set of brand-new commits with new hashes and moved the branch label to point at them. The old commits didn't get edited... they got replaced and abandoned. Oh. And everything my teammates did yesterday has parent pointers into the ABANDONED line.

There it is. Your teammates' local work is built on ancestors that origin/develop no longer acknowledges — their commits are grandchildren of ghosts. That's exactly the two symptoms: 'diverged' (their line and your new line share no recent history), and Kwesi's duplicates (his pull tried to merge the ghost line with your replacement line — same changes, different hashes, so git treats them as unrelated commits that happen to collide). And Abena's 'gone' work: origin's branch label now points at your new line, so her commits are unreachable FROM THE LABEL — invisible but not destroyed, which is why reflog rescues them. So: was the sin the rebase, or the force-push? Be precise — this determines what you're allowed to do in the future.
